claim: Cardiac macrophages increased the expression of Mmp14 (MT1-MMP) 7 days post-MI.
source: We demonstrated that cardiac Mφs increased the expression of Mmp14 (MT1-MMP) 7 days post-MI.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from sorted macrophages at different time points post-MI shown in Figure 1A, demonstrating peak Mmp14 expression at day 7.

claim: MI induced expression of Mmp2 in cardiac macrophages, reaching maximum levels at day 7 post-MI.
source: MI induced expression of Mmp14 (MT1-MMP) and its substrates Mmp2 and Col1a1 in Mφs in the heart, reaching maximum levels of expression on day 7 post-MI.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1A showing temporal expression patterns.

claim: MI induced expression of Col1a1 in cardiac macrophages, reaching maximum levels at day 7 post-MI.
source: MI induced expression of Mmp14 (MT1-MMP) and its substrates Mmp2 and Col1a1 in Mφs in the heart, reaching maximum levels of expression on day 7 post-MI.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1A showing temporal expression patterns.

claim: Mmp9 was downregulated in cardiac macrophages after infarction.
source: In contrast, other MMP family members (Mmp9 and Mmp13) were downregulated after infarction.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1A showing decreased expression post-MI.

claim: Mmp13 was downregulated in cardiac macrophages after infarction.
source: In contrast, other MMP family members (Mmp9 and Mmp13) were downregulated after infarction.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1A showing decreased expression post-MI.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showed attenuated post-MI cardiac dysfunction compared to WT mice.
source: This conditional KO (MAC-Mmp14 KO) resulted in attenuated post-MI cardiac dysfunction, reduced fibrosis, and preserved cardiac capillary network.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data showing higher LVEF in MAC-Mmp14 KO mice (Figure 1C).

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showed reduced fibrosis post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: This conditional KO (MAC-Mmp14 KO) resulted in attenuated post-MI cardiac dysfunction, reduced fibrosis, and preserved cardiac capillary network.
evidence: Supported by SHG imaging showing reduced collagen density in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 1F-G).

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showed preserved cardiac capillary network post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: This conditional KO (MAC-Mmp14 KO) resulted in attenuated post-MI cardiac dysfunction, reduced fibrosis, and preserved cardiac capillary network.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy and automated 3D analysis showing higher vascular volume density and capillary numbers (Figure 2A-B, Table 3).

claim: MT1-MMP activates latent TGFβ1 in macrophages.
source: Mechanistically, we showed that MT1-MMP activates latent TGFβ1 in Mφs, leading to paracrine SMAD2-mediated signaling in endothelial cells (ECs) and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing increased LAP-TGFβ1 on MAC-Mmp14 KO macrophages (Figure 3B-C), Western blot data (Figure 3D-E), and luciferase assays showing reduced active TGFβ1 from KO macrophages (Figure 3F-G).

claim: MT1-MMP-mediated TGFβ1 activation leads to paracrine SMAD2-mediated signaling in endothelial cells.
source: Mechanistically, we showed that MT1-MMP activates latent TGFβ1 in Mφs, leading to paracrine SMAD2-mediated signaling in endothelial cells (ECs) and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing reduced pSMAD2 in ECs from MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 4B-C).

claim: MT1-MMP-mediated TGFβ1 activation leads to endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT).
source: Mechanistically, we showed that MT1-MMP activates latent TGFβ1 in Mφs, leading to paracrine SMAD2-mediated signaling in endothelial cells (ECs) and endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing fewer CD31+PDGFRβ+ transitioning cells in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 5A-B) and in vitro co-culture experiments (Figure 6C-D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts contained fewer cells undergoing EndMT than WT hearts.
source: Post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts contained fewer cells undergoing EndMT than their wild-type counterparts, and Mmp14-deficient Mφs showed a reduced ability to induce EndMT in co-cultures with ECs.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced CD31+PDGFRβ+ cells in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 5A-B).

claim: Mmp14-deficient macrophages showed a reduced ability to induce EndMT in co-cultures with endothelial cells.
source: Post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts contained fewer cells undergoing EndMT than their wild-type counterparts, and Mmp14-deficient Mφs showed a reduced ability to induce EndMT in co-cultures with ECs.
evidence: Supported by in vitro co-culture experiments showing maintained CD31 expression and lack of SMA acquisition in MAECs co-cultured with MAC-Mmp14 KO macrophages (Figure 6C-D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had significantly higher LVEF at 28 days post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: Echocardiography revealed that Mφ-inactivation of Mmp14 ameliorated LV dysfunction and prevented LV dilation post-MI, with MAC-Mmp14 KO mice having a significantly higher LV ejection fraction (LVEF) and lower LV end-diastolic volume (LVVold) (Figure 1B–C, and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had lower LV end-diastolic volume (LVVold) at 28 days post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: Echocardiography revealed that Mφ-inactivation of Mmp14 ameliorated LV dysfunction and prevented LV dilation post-MI, with MAC-Mmp14 KO mice having a significantly higher LV ejection fraction (LVEF) and lower LV end-diastolic volume (LVVold) (Figure 1B–C, and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LAD-ligation produced smaller infarcts in MAC-Mmp14 KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: This analysis showed that LAD-ligation produced smaller infarcts and a lower WMSI in MAC-Mmp14 KO mice (Figure 1D–E), indicating better preservation of cardiac function and less pronounced wall-motion abnormalities in the LV when Mφ MT1-MMP was absent.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography-based infarct size measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had lower wall motion score index (WMSI) post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: This analysis showed that LAD-ligation produced smaller infarcts and a lower WMSI in MAC-Mmp14 KO mice (Figure 1D–E), indicating better preservation of cardiac function and less pronounced wall-motion abnormalities in the LV when Mφ MT1-MMP was absent.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography-based WMSI measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO infarcted hearts showed less-organized and sparse collagen structure compared to WT hearts.
source: SHG images of the infarct zone (IZ) revealed a highly directional and organized collagen fibril morphology in the WT infarcted group, whereas a less-organized and sparse collagen structure was observed in MAC-Mmp14 KO infarcted hearts (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by SHG microscopy images shown in Figure 1F.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO infarcted hearts showed marked drop in fibrillary collagen density compared to WT hearts.
source: Quantification of SHG signals revealed a marked drop in fibrillary collagen density in MAC-Mmp14 KO infarcted hearts (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by quantification of SHG signal shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showed augmented skewness and kurtosis of collagen fibrils, indicating thinner and underdeveloped, disarrayed collagen fibers.
source: In addition, the analysis of first-order features of collagen fibrils in SHG images showed augmented skewness and kurtosis in MAC-Mmp14 KO mice, indicating thinner and underdeveloped, disarrayed collagen fibers and thus lower tissue stiffness (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of SHG images shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had significantly higher LVEF after ischemia/reperfusion compared to WT mice.
source: Similar to the permanent occlusion model, transient ischemia impaired LV function in both genotypes, but MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had a significantly higher LVEF and lower LV end-systolic and end-diastolic internal diameters (LVIDs and LVIDd, respectively), indicating better preserved LV function and prevention of LV dilation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had lower LVIDs after ischemia/reperfusion compared to WT mice.
source: Similar to the permanent occlusion model, transient ischemia impaired LV function in both genotypes, but MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had a significantly higher LVEF and lower LV end-systolic and end-diastolic internal diameters (LVIDs and LVIDd, respectively), indicating better preserved LV function and prevention of LV dilation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had lower LVIDd after ischemia/reperfusion compared to WT mice.
source: Similar to the permanent occlusion model, transient ischemia impaired LV function in both genotypes, but MAC-Mmp14 KO mice had a significantly higher LVEF and lower LV end-systolic and end-diastolic internal diameters (LVIDs and LVIDd, respectively), indicating better preserved LV function and prevention of LV dilation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SHG imaging after I/R revealed a weaker fibrotic response with thinner and sparser collagen fibers in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts compared to WT hearts.
source: Moreover, SHG imaging analysis after I/R revealed a weaker fibrotic response, with thinner and sparser collagen fibers in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by SHG microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C.

claim: Mmp14 inactivation does not affect macrophage polarization.
source: No differences in Mφ polarization were found between WT and KO BMDMs, suggesting that Mmp14 inactivation does not affect the Mφ M1/M2 activation spectrum.
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of M1 and M2 markers in activated BMDMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) and cardiac macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts had higher vascular volume density than WT hearts.
source: MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts had a higher vascular volume density and more capillaries and ECs within the infarction than WT hearts (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by automated 3D microvasculature analysis shown in Figure 2B and Table 3.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts had more capillaries within the infarction than WT hearts.
source: MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts had a higher vascular volume density and more capillaries and ECs within the infarction than WT hearts (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by automated 3D microvasculature analysis shown in Figure 2B and Table 3.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts had more endothelial cells within the infarction than WT hearts.
source: MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts had a higher vascular volume density and more capillaries and ECs within the infarction than WT hearts (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by automated 3D microvasculature analysis shown in Figure 2B and Table 3.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts showed increased capillary density and reduced intercapillary and diffusion distances post-MI.
source: Accordingly, in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts, we observed increased capillary density and reduced intercapillary and diffusion distances, parameters proposed as indices of oxygen diffusion (Gkontra et al., 2018), suggesting better oxygen diffusion in the infarcted myocardium (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by automated 3D microvasculature analysis shown in Figure 2B and Table 3, with citation to established methodology.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts showed a smaller CA-IX+ area in the infarction at 7 days post-MI compared to WT hearts.
source: Next, we assessed hypoxia in the post LAD-ligation myocardium by carbonic anhydrase IX (CA-IX) staining (Figure 2C), which revealed a smaller CA-IX+ area in the infarction of 7-day-post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts than in WT counterparts (Figure 2C–D), confirming better-preserved tissue oxygenation after MI.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO Mφs had higher content of LAP and TGFβ1 on their surface compared to WT Mφs.
source: KO Mφs had a higher content of LAP and TGFβ1, revealing significantly higher surface retention of LAP-TGFβ1 than observed in WT Mφs (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Latent TGFβ1 (~50 kDa) preferentially located in the membrane and was more abundant in Mmp14-deficient Mφs.
source: Latent TGFβ1 (~50 kDa) consisting of LAP (35 kDa) covalently bound to the mature TGFβ1 (12.5 kDa) preferentially located in the membrane and was more abundant in Mmp14-deficient Mφs (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of subcellular fractions shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: There was no difference in Tgfb1 transcript levels between WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs.
source: In line with the reported role of MT1-MMP in the posttranslational processing of pro-TGFβ1, we found no difference in Tgfb1 transcript levels between WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F, with inference based on known MT1-MMP function.

claim: Active TGFβ1 was undetectable after co-culture of HEK293 cells with MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs.
source: HEK293 co-culture with WT BMDMs produced abundant levels of active TGFβ1, whereas active TGFβ1 was undetectable after co-culture with MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: MT1-MMP-dependent TGFβ1 activation requires MT1-MMP catalytic activity.
source: TGFβ1 levels in MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs were restored by transduction with full-length (FL) MT1-MMP but not with a catalytic mutant (E240A), demonstrating that MT1-MMP-dependent TGFβ1 activation requires MT1-MMP catalytic activity (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data with lentiviral rescue experiments shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There was no between-genotype difference in pSMAD2 abundance in macrophages at 7 days post-MI.
source: There was no between-genotype difference in pSMAD2 abundance in Mφs; however, pSMAD2 was significantly less abundant in ECs and MyoFBs/VSMCs from MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 4B–C), suggesting that lack of Mφ MT1-MMP impairs paracrine TGFβ1-pSMAD2 signaling in ECs and MyoFBs/VSMCs.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: pSMAD2 was significantly less abundant in endothelial cells from MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts compared to WT hearts at 7 days post-MI.
source: There was no between-genotype difference in pSMAD2 abundance in Mφs; however, pSMAD2 was significantly less abundant in ECs and MyoFBs/VSMCs from MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 4B–C), suggesting that lack of Mφ MT1-MMP impairs paracrine TGFβ1-pSMAD2 signaling in ECs and MyoFBs/VSMCs.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: pSMAD2 was significantly less abundant in MyoFBs/VSMCs from MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts compared to WT hearts at 7 days post-MI.
source: There was no between-genotype difference in pSMAD2 abundance in Mφs; however, pSMAD2 was significantly less abundant in ECs and MyoFBs/VSMCs from MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 4B–C), suggesting that lack of Mφ MT1-MMP impairs paracrine TGFβ1-pSMAD2 signaling in ECs and MyoFBs/VSMCs.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: pSMAD2-positive myofibroblasts were less abundant in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts than in WT hearts at 7 days post-MI.
source: To distinguish between pSMAD2 in MyoFBs (non-vascular-related SMA+ cells) and VSMCs (vascular-related SMA+ cells), we performed confocal imaging analysis at 7 days post-MI which revealed that pSMAD2-positive MyoFBs and VSMCs were both less abundant in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts than in WT hearts (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: pSMAD2-positive VSMCs were less abundant in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts than in WT hearts at 7 days post-MI.
source: To distinguish between pSMAD2 in MyoFBs (non-vascular-related SMA+ cells) and VSMCs (vascular-related SMA+ cells), we performed confocal imaging analysis at 7 days post-MI which revealed that pSMAD2-positive MyoFBs and VSMCs were both less abundant in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts than in WT hearts (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showed fewer macrophages in the infarcted myocardium at 7 days post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: We found that Mφ MT1-MMP inactivation altered the cellular composition of the infarcted myocardium, with MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showing fewer Mφs, indicating a less inflammatory state; more ECs, in line with the microvasculature image analysis data; and fewer MyoFBs, in agreement with the reduced fibrotic response (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showed more endothelial cells in the infarcted myocardium at 7 days post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: We found that Mφ MT1-MMP inactivation altered the cellular composition of the infarcted myocardium, with MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showing fewer Mφs, indicating a less inflammatory state; more ECs, in line with the microvasculature image analysis data; and fewer MyoFBs, in agreement with the reduced fibrotic response (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showed fewer myofibroblasts in the infarcted myocardium at 7 days post-MI compared to WT mice.
source: We found that Mφ MT1-MMP inactivation altered the cellular composition of the infarcted myocardium, with MAC-Mmp14 KO mice showing fewer Mφs, indicating a less inflammatory state; more ECs, in line with the microvasculature image analysis data; and fewer MyoFBs, in agreement with the reduced fibrotic response (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: An intermediary population of cells with mild levels of both CD31 and PDGFRβ was detected in post-MI hearts.
source: Additionally, we detected an intermediary population of cells with mild levels of both CD31 (endothelial marker) and PDGFRβ (mesenchymal marker) (Figure 5A). This population is suggestive of transitioning cells undergoing endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT) (Aisagbonhi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A, with citation to previous work identifying such populations.

claim: Endothelial-cell derived Tomato+ cells were found within the myofibroblast compartment in 7-day-post-MI hearts from Cdh5-CreERT2 R26Tomato mice.
source: To confirm the occurrence of EndMT in the context of MI, we performed lineage tracing experiments in Cdh5-CreERT2 R26Tomato control and infarcted mice and asked whether we could find endothelial-cell derived Tomato+ cells within the MyoFB compartment using flow cytometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–E). We detected an increase in Tomato+PDGFRβ+ cells in 7-day-post-MI hearts (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E), confirming that EndMT is triggered upon MI as previously reported (Aisagbonhi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-E, with citation to previous work.

claim: CD31+PDGFRβ+ cells showed loss of endothelial markers and acquisition of mesenchymal genes.
source: We confirmed the transitioning phenotype of CD31+PDGFRβ+ cells by qPCR and observed the loss of endothelial markers (i.e. Pecam, Cdh5, Kdr, Tie2, Col4a2), the acquisition of mesenchymal genes (i.e. Cdh2, Tagln, Col1a1, Col1a2, Col3a1), and the upregulation of EndMT-mediating transcriptional factors (i.e. Zeb2 and Snai1) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of sorted cell populations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD31+PDGFRβ+ cells showed upregulation of EndMT-mediating transcriptional factors Zeb2 and Snai1.
source: We confirmed the transitioning phenotype of CD31+PDGFRβ+ cells by qPCR and observed the loss of endothelial markers (i.e. Pecam, Cdh5, Kdr, Tie2, Col4a2), the acquisition of mesenchymal genes (i.e. Cdh2, Tagln, Col1a1, Col1a2, Col3a1), and the upregulation of EndMT-mediating transcriptional factors (i.e. Zeb2 and Snai1) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of sorted cell populations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD31+PDGFRβ+ transitioning cells were less abundant in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts compared to WT hearts.
source: Interestingly, these cells were less abundant in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts (Figure 5A–B), suggesting that EndMT is impaired in the absence of Mφ MT1-MMP.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Triple positive cells for ERG, SMA, and pSMAD2 were found in the infarcted cardiac tissue.
source: We found by immunofluorescence triple-positive cells for the endothelial nuclear marker ERG, the mesenchymal marker SMA and pSMAD2, reflecting the transition of endothelial cells towards a mesenchymal phenotype via SMAD2 activation in the infarcted cardiac tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-D.

claim: MAECs co-cultured with WT BMDMs progressively lost their cobblestone appearance and adopted a dispersed, spindle-shaped morphology.
source: The immunofluorescence analysis with the endothelial marker CD31 and the mesenchymal marker SMA revealed morphological changes in MAECs after co-culture with WT BMDMs, with cells progressively losing their cobblestone appearance and adopting a dispersed, spindle-shaped morphology (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MAECs co-cultured with WT BMDMs significantly decreased CD31 expression and acquired SMA expression.
source: Moreover, MAECs co-cultured with WT BMDMs significantly decreased CD31 expression and acquired SMA expression, indicating the acquisition of molecular traits of a mesenchymal phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Co-culture of MAECs with MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs led neither to the loss of endothelial features nor to the acquisition of mesenchymal markers.
source: By contrast, co-culture of MAECs with MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs led neither to the loss of endothelial features nor to the acquisition of mesenchymal markers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Treatment of MAEC-BMDM co-cultures with a neutralizing anti-TGFβ1 antibody blocked EndMT.
source: Treatment of MAEC-BMDM co-cultures with a neutralizing anti-TGFβ1 antibody blocked EndMT, demonstrating that Mφs induced EndMT via MT1-MMP/TGFβ1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification with antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Co-culture of MAECs with WT BMDMs caused downregulation of EC-related genes (Pecam, Kdr, and Col4a2).
source: In accordance with the immunofluorescence data, the co-culture of MAECs with WT BMDMs caused the downregulation of EC-related genes (Pecam, Kdr, and Col4a2) and the upregulation of mesenchymal genes (Tagln and Acta2) and the direct TGFβ1 target Serpine1 (Pai1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-culture of MAECs with WT BMDMs caused upregulation of mesenchymal genes (Tagln and Acta2).
source: In accordance with the immunofluorescence data, the co-culture of MAECs with WT BMDMs caused the downregulation of EC-related genes (Pecam, Kdr, and Col4a2) and the upregulation of mesenchymal genes (Tagln and Acta2) and the direct TGFβ1 target Serpine1 (Pai1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-culture of MAECs with WT BMDMs caused upregulation of the direct TGFβ1 target Serpine1 (Pai1).
source: In accordance with the immunofluorescence data, the co-culture of MAECs with WT BMDMs caused the downregulation of EC-related genes (Pecam, Kdr, and Col4a2) and the upregulation of mesenchymal genes (Tagln and Acta2) and the direct TGFβ1 target Serpine1 (Pai1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changes toward a mesenchymal phenotype in MAECs were not triggered by co-culture with MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs.
source: By contrast, these changes toward a mesenchymal phenotype in MAECs were not triggered by co-culture with MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: LAP and TGFβ1 were both significantly increased on the surface of MAC-Mmp14 KO cardiac Mφs after MI.
source: LAP and TGFβ1 were both significantly increased on the surface of MAC-Mmp14 KO Mφs after MI, indicating the retention of latent TGFβ1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from cardiac macrophages shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Post-MI WT cardiac Mφs produced detectable levels of active TGFβ1.
source: As with BMDMs, post-MI WT cardiac Mφs produced detectable levels of active TGFβ1, whereas the inactivation of Mmp14 in Mφs abrogated TGFβ1 activation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay with sorted cardiac macrophages shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inactivation of Mmp14 in cardiac Mφs abrogated TGFβ1 activation.
source: As with BMDMs, post-MI WT cardiac Mφs produced detectable levels of active TGFβ1, whereas the inactivation of Mmp14 in Mφs abrogated TGFβ1 activation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay with sorted cardiac macrophages shown in Figure 6B.

claim: WT cardiac Mφs induced EndMT in MAECs, downregulating CD31 expression and increasing SMA expression.
source: In co-culture experiments, WT cardiac Mφs induced EndMT in MAECs, downregulating CD31 expression, and increasing SMA expression. By contrast, no transition to a mesenchymal phenotype was evident in MAECs co-cultured with Mmp14-deficient cardiac Mφs (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification of co-cultures shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: No transition to a mesenchymal phenotype was evident in MAECs co-cultured with Mmp14-deficient cardiac Mφs.
source: In co-culture experiments, WT cardiac Mφs induced EndMT in MAECs, downregulating CD31 expression, and increasing SMA expression. By contrast, no transition to a mesenchymal phenotype was evident in MAECs co-cultured with Mmp14-deficient cardiac Mφs (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification of co-cultures shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Myocardial infarction continues to be one of the most lethal diseases worldwide.
source: Although the mortality rate from cardiovascular disease (CVD) has declined over the last 50 years, myocardial infarction (MI) continues to be one of the most lethal diseases worldwide, and many pathologies arise from adverse remodeling after cardiac injury (e.g. heart failure and cardiac rupture) (Benjamin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Many pathologies arise from adverse remodeling after cardiac injury, including heart failure and cardiac rupture.
source: Although the mortality rate from cardiovascular disease (CVD) has declined over the last 50 years, myocardial infarction (MI) continues to be one of the most lethal diseases worldwide, and many pathologies arise from adverse remodeling after cardiac injury (e.g. heart failure and cardiac rupture) (Benjamin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: MI is usually provoked by plaque rupture in a coronary artery, resulting in insufficient oxygen supply to the myocardium.
source: MI is usually provoked by plaque rupture in a coronary artery, resulting in insufficient oxygen supply to the myocardium, which undergoes necrosis.
evidence: Based on established medical knowledge of MI pathophysiology.

claim: The onset of MI triggers a cascade of events, including cardiomyocyte death, acute inflammation, angiogenesis, and scar formation.
source: The onset of MI triggers a cascade of events, including cardiomyocyte (CM) death, acute inflammation, angiogenesis, and scar formation (Frangogiannis, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to review of MI pathophysiology.

claim: Cardiac healing is impaired by both excessive and insufficient expansion of macrophages.
source: Cardiac healing is impaired by both excessive and insufficient expansion of macrophages (Mφs), prompting interest in the potential of Mφs as therapeutic targets for CVD (Dick et al., 2019; Panizzi et al., 2010; van Amerongen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating this relationship.

claim: Post-injury Mφs are distinct from resident cardiac Mφs.
source: We and others have shown that post-injury Mφs are distinct from resident cardiac Mφs (Bajpai et al., 2019; Dick et al., 2019; Walter et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies including the authors' own work.

claim: Monocytes and Mφs are sequentially mobilized from bone marrow and spleen to the infarcted myocardium.
source: Monocytes and Mφs are sequentially mobilized from bone marrow (BM) and spleen to the infarcted myocardium (Nahrendorf et al., 2007; Swirski et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating macrophage recruitment.

claim: During day 1 to day 4 after injury, Ly6Chigh inflammatory Mφs clear necrotic cellular debris and damaged extracellular matrix from the tissue.
source: During day 1 to day 4 after injury, Ly6Chigh inflammatory Mφs clear necrotic cellular debris and damaged extracellular matrix (ECM) from the tissue and attract other immune cells through the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL1β, and IL6) that further fuel inflammation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of macrophage function post-MI.

claim: Ly6Clow reparative Mφs have the capacity to dampen inflammation, promote ECM reconstruction, and angiogenesis.
source: Over the course of several days, the inflammatory phase gives way to a healing phase, dominated by the second wave of Mφs, this time Ly6Clow reparative Mφs with the capacity to dampen inflammation, promote ECM reconstruction, and angiogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of macrophage function post-MI.

claim: Ly6Clow reparative Mφs are characterized by the secretion of anti-inflammatory (IL10), angiogenic (VEGF), and pro-fibrotic (TGFβ1) factors, as well as matrix metalloproteinases.
source: These latter Mφs are characterized by the secretion of anti-inflammatory (IL10), angiogenic (VEGF), and pro-fibrotic (TGFβ1) factors, as well as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which promote tissue remodeling (Nahrendorf et al., 2007; Walter et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing macrophage phenotypes.

claim: MMPs are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases that have been traditionally associated with the degradation and turnover of ECM components.
source: MMPs are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases that have been traditionally associated with the degradation and turnover of ECM components.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of MMP biochemistry.

claim: MMPs directly and indirectly regulate cell behavior and microenvironment through the proteolytic processing of a large variety of molecules, such as membrane receptors and growth factors.
source: MMPs are now known to, directly and indirectly, regulate cell behavior and microenvironment through the proteolytic processing of a large variety of molecules, such as membrane receptors and growth factors (Page-McCaw et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to review of MMP functions.

claim: MT1-MMP was the first membrane-anchored MMP to be described.
source: Membrane type 1 matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP/Mmp14) was the first membrane-anchored MMP to be described (Sato et al., 1994), and the cell surface location provides this enzyme with exclusive functions affecting cellular behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to the original description of MT1-MMP.

claim: MT1-MMP is involved in the degradation of a spectrum of structural matrix proteins including collagens I, II, and III, fibronectin, and laminin.
source: MT1-MMP is involved in the degradation of a spectrum of structural matrix proteins (including collagens I, II, and III, fibronectin, and laminin), the proteolytic processing of growth factors and cytokines (e.g. TGFβ and SDF-1), and the activation of other MMPs (e.g. pro-MMP2), expanding MT1-MMP functional pleiotropism.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of MT1-MMP substrates.

claim: MT1-MMP is involved in the proteolytic processing of growth factors and cytokines such as TGFβ and SDF-1.
source: MT1-MMP is involved in the degradation of a spectrum of structural matrix proteins (including collagens I, II, and III, fibronectin, and laminin), the proteolytic processing of growth factors and cytokines (e.g. TGFβ and SDF-1), and the activation of other MMPs (e.g. pro-MMP2), expanding MT1-MMP functional pleiotropism.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of MT1-MMP substrates.

claim: MT1-MMP is involved in the activation of other MMPs such as pro-MMP2.
source: MT1-MMP is involved in the degradation of a spectrum of structural matrix proteins (including collagens I, II, and III, fibronectin, and laminin), the proteolytic processing of growth factors and cytokines (e.g. TGFβ and SDF-1), and the activation of other MMPs (e.g. pro-MMP2), expanding MT1-MMP functional pleiotropism.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of MT1-MMP substrates.

claim: Previous studies pointed out a deleterious role of MT1-MMP in post-MI cardiac remodeling, mostly related to its collagenase activity in fibroblasts.
source: Previous studies pointed out a deleterious role of MT1-MMP in post-MI cardiac remodeling, mostly related to its collagenase activity in fibroblasts (FBs) (Koenig et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Specific Mφ MT1-MMP contribution to cardiac healing response has never been addressed before this study.
source: Nevertheless, specific Mφ MT1-MMP contribution to cardiac healing response has never been addressed.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Mmp14 was efficiently inactivated in BM-derived Mφs from MAC-Mmp14 KO mice.
source: Mmp14 was efficiently inactivated in BM-derived Mφs (BMDMs) and in cardiac Mφs sorted from 7-day-post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts; in contrast, Mmp14 expression did not differ between endothelial cells (ECs) purified from WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Mmp14 was efficiently inactivated in cardiac Mφs sorted from 7-day-post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts.
source: Mmp14 was efficiently inactivated in BM-derived Mφs (BMDMs) and in cardiac Mφs sorted from 7-day-post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts; in contrast, Mmp14 expression did not differ between endothelial cells (ECs) purified from WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Mmp14 expression did not differ between endothelial cells purified from WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts.
source: Mmp14 was efficiently inactivated in BM-derived Mφs (BMDMs) and in cardiac Mφs sorted from 7-day-post-MI MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts; in contrast, Mmp14 expression did not differ between endothelial cells (ECs) purified from WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO 7-day-post-MI hearts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There were no significant differences in baseline cardiac function between WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO mice.
source: No significant differences in either baseline cardiac function (Table 1) or in circulating monocytes and neutrophils were found between genotypes (Table 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography and electrocardiography data shown in Table 1.

claim: There were no significant differences in circulating monocytes and neutrophils between WT and MAC-Mmp14 KO mice.
source: No significant differences in either baseline cardiac function (Table 1) or in circulating monocytes and neutrophils were found between genotypes (Table 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by hematogram data shown in Table 2 and flow cytometry in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: TGFβ is considered the master mediator of EndMT, in a SMAD-dependent manner.
source: TGFβ is considered the master mediator of EndMT, in a SMAD-dependent manner (Frangogiannis, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to review of EndMT mechanisms.

claim: The contribution of EndMT to cardiac fibrosis depends on the nature of the cardiovascular injury and the extent of the fibrosis.
source: The contribution of EndMT to cardiac fibrosis remains however a matter of debate, which depends on the nature of the cardiovascular injury and the extent of the fibrosis (Aisagbonhi et al., 2011; Evrard et al., 2016; Kanisicak et al., 2016; Moore-Morris et al., 2014; Zeisberg et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies with varying findings.

claim: EndMT is minimal in pressure overload or I/R models, where the intensity of inflammatory and fibrotic responses is much lower than after acute ischemic injury.
source: For example, EndMT is minimal in pressure overload or I/R models, where the intensity of inflammatory and fibrotic responses is much lower than after acute ischemic injury (Moore-Morris et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies comparing different injury models.

claim: MT1-MMP has been identified as an activator of epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) in development, cancer, and lung fibrosis.
source: Our findings are in line with the role of MT1-MMP as an activator of epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) in other pathophysiological contexts such as development, cancer, and lung fibrosis (Garmon et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in other disease contexts.

claim: A recent scRNAseq study identified a subset of post-MI Mφs with a HIF1α-dependent signature that specifically upregulated Mmp14 expression.
source: Interestingly, a recent scRNAseq study carried out on healthy and post-infarcted hearts identified a subset of post-MI Mφs with a HIF1α-dependent signature, which specifically upregulated Mmp14 expression (Dick et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to single-cell RNA sequencing study.

claim: Macrophages have been reported as inducers of EndMT in atherosclerosis.
source: Moreover, Mφs have recently been reported as inducers of EndMT in atherosclerosis (Helmke et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to study in atherosclerosis.

claim: Treatment with menstrual-blood–derived mesenchymal stem cells has been shown to protect endothelial function, reduce infarct size, decrease cardiac fibrosis, and downregulate TGFβ1/SMAD signaling through the comprehensive inhibition of EndMT in an experimental rat model of MI.
source: Interestingly, in an experimental rat model of MI, treatment with menstrual-blood–derived mesenchymal stem cells has been shown to protect endothelial function, reduce infarct size, decrease cardiac fibrosis, and downregulate TGFβ1/SMAD signaling, all through the comprehensive inhibition of EndMT (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to stem cell therapy study.

claim: Selective MT1-MMP inhibition rescued tissue damage and mortality in influenza-infected mice.
source: A recent study reported that selective MT1-MMP inhibition rescued tissue damage and mortality in influenza-infected mice, demonstrating the potential of specific MT1-MMP inhibitors to ameliorate the detrimental effects of this protease on tissue remodeling (Talmi-Frank et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to study in influenza model.

claim: Excessive MMP activity after MI and subsequent ECM turnover can result in adverse remodeling and worsened cardiac dysfunction.
source: Although ECM remodeling and granulation tissue formation are prerequisites for tissue repair, excessive MMP activity after MI and subsequent ECM turnover can result in adverse remodeling and worsened cardiac dysfunction (Spinale et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to review of MMP function in cardiac remodeling.

claim: A detrimental role of MT1-MMP in post-MI cardiac remodeling has been identified using mouse infarct models, leading to worsening cardiac function and reduced survival.
source: A detrimental role of MT1-MMP in post-MI cardiac remodeling has been identified using mouse infarct models, leading to worsening cardiac function and reduced survival (Koenig et al., 2012; Spinale et al., 2010; Zavadzkas et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple mouse studies.

claim: Previous studies attributed the detrimental role of MT1-MMP in post-MI remodeling to its collagenase activity in fibroblasts.
source: These studies attributed this detrimental role to MT1-MMP collagenase activity in FBs, disregarding its actions in Mφs (Koenig et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Pro-TGFβ has been recognized as a target for MT1-MMP–mediated cleavage in several contexts.
source: Pro-TGFβ has been recognized as a target for MT1-MMP–mediated cleavage in several contexts (Koziol et al., 2012; Mu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating MT1-MMP cleavage of TGFβ.

claim: Previous studies identified MT1-MMP as an inducer of fibrosis through its cleavage of latent-transforming growth factor beta-binding protein 1 (LTBP1) and activation of TGFβ-mediated SMAD2/3 signaling in the infarcted myocardium.
source: Previous studies identified MT1-MMP as an inducer of fibrosis through its cleavage of latent-transforming growth factor beta-binding protein 1 (LTBP1) and activation of TGFβ-mediated SMAD2/3 signaling in the infarcted myocardium (Spinale et al., 2010; Zavadzkas et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism.

claim: TGFβ1 is the main driver of FB differentiation to MyoFBs.
source: TGFβ1 is the main driver of FB differentiation to MyoFBs (van den Borne et al., 2010); our results, showing reduced MyoFBs numbers in MAC-Mmp14 KO hearts and depressed Serpine1 expression by FBs treated with MAC-Mmp14 KO Mφs, suggest that MT1-MMP plays a role in MyoFB activation via TGFβ1.
evidence: Supported by citation to study of fibroblast differentiation, combined with data from this study.

claim: TGFβ-mediated EndMT has been identified during cardiac fibrosis and contributes to collagen matrix deposition and disease.
source: TGFβ-mediated EndMT has been identified during cardiac fibrosis (Zeisberg et al., 2007) and contributes to collagen matrix deposition and disease.
evidence: Supported by citation to study identifying EndMT in cardiac fibrosis.

claim: EndMT is essential for cardiac valve formation and vascular development in embryogenic stages.
source: EndMT is essential for cardiac valve formation and vascular development in embryogenic stages as well as in the pathogenesis of diverse cardiovascular disorders, such as congenital heart disease (Hofmann et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: Hypoxia is a well-known stimulus for EndMT.
source: The Mmp14 expression in these cells converges with a hypoxia-driven program, which represents a well-known stimulus for EndMT (Evrard et al., 2016), further supporting the implication of Mmp14-expressing post-MI Mφs in EndMT.
evidence: Supported by citation to study of hypoxia and EndMT.

claim: MT1-MMP promotes TGFβ1 activation via integrin αvβ8 at the cell surface.
source: It has been shown that MT1-MMP promotes TGFβ1 activation via integrin αvβ8 at the cell surface (Mu et al., 2002), and that TGFβ1 modulates myocardial healing through effects on the fibrotic and angiogenic responses (Frangogiannis, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: TGFβ1 modulates myocardial healing through effects on the fibrotic and angiogenic responses.
source: It has been shown that MT1-MMP promotes TGFβ1 activation via integrin αvβ8 at the cell surface (Mu et al., 2002), and that TGFβ1 modulates myocardial healing through effects on the fibrotic and angiogenic responses (Frangogiannis, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to review of TGFβ1 function in cardiac healing.

claim: Active TGFβ1 has an estimated half-life of 2–3 min.
source: Since active TGFβ1 has an estimated half-life of 2–3 min, and only 2–5% of total TGFβ1 is thought to be activated at any given time (Lawrence, 2001), we measured bioactive TGFβ1 using a standardized luciferase assay (Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by citation to study of TGFβ1 biochemistry.

claim: Only 2–5% of total TGFβ1 is thought to be activated at any given time.
source: Since active TGFβ1 has an estimated half-life of 2–3 min, and only 2–5% of total TGFβ1 is thought to be activated at any given time (Lawrence, 2001), we measured bioactive TGFβ1 using a standardized luciferase assay (Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by citation to study of TGFβ1 biochemistry.

claim: PDGFRβ induction is an early feature of myofibroblast activation.
source: Cardiac FBs convert to MyoFBs with injury to mediate healing after MI and platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ) induction is an early feature of MyoFB activation (Henderson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to study of myofibroblast markers.

claim: Serpine1 expression was significantly higher in FBs treated with conditioned medium from WT BMDMs compared to MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs.
source: qPCR analysis of cardiac FBs and CMs after culture with supernatants from LPS-activated WT or MAC-Mmp14 KO BMDMs revealed no changes except for the direct TGFβ1 gene target Serpine1, whose expression was significantly higher in FBs treated with conditioned medium from WT BMDMs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Oxygen diffusion from blood to tissue critically depends on the density and arrangement of the microvascular bed.
source: Oxygen diffusion from blood to tissue critically depends on the density and arrangement of the microvascular bed.
evidence: Based on established physiological principles.

claim: The small latent complex (SLC) consisting of latency associated peptide (LAP) and mature TGFβ1 can be retained at the cell surface through LAP binding to membrane receptors such as integrin αvβ8.
source: The small latent complex (SLC) consisting of latency associated peptide (LAP) and mature TGFβ1 can be retained at the cell surface through LAP binding to membrane receptors (e.g. integrin αvβ8) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TGFβ1 biology, illustrated in Figure 3A.
